# Using OpenGL ES 3.0+ in Kanzi[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/rendering/using-opengl-es-30.html#using-opengl-es-3-0-in-k "Link to this heading")
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/copy-to-clipboard.svg) Copy page ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/arrow-down.svg)
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/copy-to-clipboard.svg) Copy page
Copy this page as Markdown for LLMs.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/markdown.svg) View as Markdown
View this page as Markdown.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/claude.svg) Ask Claude
Ask Claude about this topic.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/chatgpt.svg) Ask ChatGPT
Ask ChatGPT about this topic.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/vscode.svg) Connect to VS Code
Install Kanzi Documentation MCP server to VS Code.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/claude.svg) Connect to Claude
Download and run the Claude mcpb.
Kanzi supports deployment to OpenGL ES 3.0, 3.1, and 3.2. Shader **source code** in your materials must use GLSL ES version 310 or later syntax regardless of the deployment target — Kanzi cross-compiles shaders to the GLSL ES dialect matching the project’s Target Graphics API setting. With OpenGL ES 3.0 and above you can use integer textures, floating point, and multiple render targets. For example, this allows you to have more precision with the rendered images, you can apply better looking post-processing effects, use HDR for textures and cubemap textures, and create seamless cubemaps. With OpenGL ES 3.1 you can additionally use compute shaders, image load/store, and shader storage buffer objects. With OpenGL ES 3.2, you can also use geometry and tessellation shaders.
Before you use OpenGL ES 3.0+, make sure that your target platform supports the API version.
To select the version of OpenGL ES to use in Kanzi:
  1. In the Kanzi Studio main menu, select Project > Properties and set the Target Graphics API to the OpenGL ES version your target platform supports: OpenGL ES 3.0, OpenGL ES 3.1, or OpenGL ES 3.2.
![../../_images/project-properties.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/project-properties.png) ![../../_images/target-graphics-api-opengl-es-30.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/target-graphics-api-opengl-es-30.png)
  2. In your shader source files, add as the first line the OpenGL ES version tag.
Kanzi requires `#version 310 es` or later as the version tag in shader source code, regardless of your Target Graphics API. Earlier tags such as `#version 300 es` are not accepted. If Target Graphics API is set to OpenGL ES 3.0, the shader is cross-compiled to `#version 300 es` at export time, provided the source does not use features that were introduced in GLSL ES 3.1 or later.
     * For shaders that do not use features introduced after GLSL ES 3.1, add

```
#version 310 es

```
Copy to clipboard
     * For shaders that use geometry or tessellation shader features (which require Target Graphics API OpenGL ES 3.2), add

```
#version 320 es

```
Copy to clipboard


## Setting the shader families to export[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/rendering/using-opengl-es-30.html#setting-the-shader-families-to-export "Link to this heading")
When Kanzi Studio exports a kzb file, it compiles shaders for the families listed in the Target Shader Family property. By default, Kanzi Studio compiles shaders for all three families: OpenGL, OpenGL ES, and Vulkan. To reduce the size of the kzb file, remove the families that your target platform does not use.
The GLSL or GLSL ES version that Kanzi Studio uses for the OpenGL and OpenGL ES families depends on the Target Graphics API setting.
Note
When Target Graphics API is Vulkan 1.2, Kanzi Studio exports only Vulkan SPIR-V shaders, regardless of the Target Shader Family setting.
To set the shader families to export:
  1. In the Kanzi Studio main menu, select Project > Properties.
  2. In the Binary Export category, set the Target Shader Family property. Click Shader family to select the families to include:
     * OpenGL — Kanzi Studio compiles GLSL shaders for OpenGL desktop platforms.
     * OpenGL ES — Kanzi Studio compiles GLSL ES shaders for OpenGL ES mobile and embedded platforms.
     * Vulkan — Kanzi Studio compiles SPIR-V shaders for Vulkan platforms.
To include multiple families, select each from the menu. Kanzi Studio shows the selected families as a comma-separated list in the property field.
![../../_images/set-target-shader-family.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/set-target-shader-family.png)


## Setting the color format of textures[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/rendering/using-opengl-es-30.html#setting-the-color-format-of-textures "Link to this heading")
You can import to your Kanzi Studio project HDR and floating point images in .dds format and set the color format of the textures that use these images.
To set the color format of textures:
  1. In the Library > Resource Files > Images, select the image whose color format you want to set.
![../../_images/library-resource-files-images.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/library-resource-files-images.png)
  2. In the Properties, set:
     * Target Format to Raw
     * Color Format in Raw to the color format that you want Kanzi to use to interpret the texture
![../../_images/target-format-raw.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/target-format-raw.png) ![../../_images/color-format-in-raw.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/color-format-in-raw.png)
  3. In the Library > Materials and Textures > `Textures`, select the texture that uses the image whose color format you set in the previous step. In the Properties, set:
     * Wrap Mode to Clamp
     * Mipmap Mode to Linear or Nearest
![../../_images/mipmapmode-linear-wrap-mode-clamp.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/mipmapmode-linear-wrap-mode-clamp.png)


## Setting the format of a render target texture[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/rendering/using-opengl-es-30.html#setting-the-format-of-a-render-target-texture "Link to this heading")
Set the format of a render target texture to define the target pixel format used by the GPU.
To set the format of a render target texture:
  1. In the Library > Materials and Textures > `Textures`, select or create a Render Target Texture.
  2. In the Properties, set the Format to the target pixel format that you want to use.
![../../_images/render-target-texture-es-30-format.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/render-target-texture-es-30-format.png)
  3. If your render target textures are in integer target format, set the Minification Filter and Magnification Filter properties to Nearest.


## Selecting runtime graphics backend[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/rendering/using-opengl-es-30.html#selecting-runtime-graphics-backend "Link to this heading")
On the Windows operating system you can select whether you want to use OpenGL ES, OpenGL, or Vulkan in the `Application::onConfigure[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a11370.html#a3803fce5a93d4211e67cc9be1d14f92c)` function, in the `application.cfg`, or using the command line arguments, if your target supports command line arguments.
On the command line use:
  * `--gles` or `--opengles` to use OpenGL ES
  * `--gl` or `--opengl` to use OpenGL
  * `--vk` or `--vulkan` to use Vulkan
  * `--egl` to use EGL
  * `--wgl` to use WGL
  * `--glx` to use GLX

  
| In `application.cfg`  |  `SurfaceClientAPI = clientApi` `GraphicsContextAPI = contextApi`  |  
| --- | --- |  
| In `Application::onConfigure[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a11370.html#a3803fce5a93d4211e67cc9be1d14f92c)`  |  `configuration.defaultSurfaceProperties.clientAPI = clientApi;` `configuration.defaultSurfaceProperties.contextAPI = contextApi;`  |  
| Values  |   
 | `clientApi`  |  To use OpenGL ES:
  * In `application.cfg` use `gles` or `opengles`.
  * In `Application::onConfigure[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a11370.html#a3803fce5a93d4211e67cc9be1d14f92c)` use `SurfaceClientAPI::OpenGLES[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a11119.html#a6559e617448fb7945ea688c318ec43a6af4b7db07e13ba92157b1b7d961abfaae)`.

To use OpenGL:
  * In `application.cfg` use `gl` or `opengl`.
  * In `Application::onConfigure[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a11370.html#a3803fce5a93d4211e67cc9be1d14f92c)` use `SurfaceClientAPI::OpenGL[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a11119.html#a6559e617448fb7945ea688c318ec43a6a760716b590ee7c0adc25f434f577d8be)`.

To use Vulkan:
  * In `application.cfg` use `vk` or `vulkan`.
  * In `Application::onConfigure[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a11370.html#a3803fce5a93d4211e67cc9be1d14f92c)` use `SurfaceClientAPI::Vulkan[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a11119.html#a6559e617448fb7945ea688c318ec43a6a38625270231b647116c80bcbc4f9d1d8)`.

 |  
| --- | --- |  
| `contextApi`  |  To use WGL:
  * In `application.cfg` use `wgl`.
  * In `Application::onConfigure[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a11370.html#a3803fce5a93d4211e67cc9be1d14f92c)` use `GraphicsContextAPI::WGL[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a11119.html#a6f5c2a73db0b2d1b65db9b192a451013aef3c7326c5c23cc9c408d29410352b67)`.

To use EGL:
  * In `application.cfg` use `egl`.
  * In `Application::onConfigure[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a11370.html#a3803fce5a93d4211e67cc9be1d14f92c)` use `GraphicsContextAPI::EGL[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a11119.html#a6f5c2a73db0b2d1b65db9b192a451013ab1e1fe0cc927dbeae22dc1839e01bb20)`.

To use GLX:
  * In `application.cfg` use `glx`.
  * In `Application::onConfigure[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a11370.html#a3803fce5a93d4211e67cc9be1d14f92c)` use `GraphicsContextAPI::GLX[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a11119.html#a6f5c2a73db0b2d1b65db9b192a451013ac313d26d26abf7402a24ce15663b52b6)`.

 |  
 |  
| `application.cfg` example  |  
```
# Sets the surface target for OpenGL rendering and WGL graphics context.
SurfaceClientAPI = gl
GraphicsContextAPI = wgl

```
Copy to clipboard  |  
| `Application::onConfigure[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a11370.html#a3803fce5a93d4211e67cc9be1d14f92c)` example  |  
```
// Sets the surface target for OpenGL rendering and WGL graphics context.
configuration.defaultSurfaceProperties.clientAPI = SurfaceClientAPI::OpenGL;
configuration.defaultSurfaceProperties.contextAPI = GraphicsContextAPI::WGL;

```
Copy to clipboard  |  
## Enabling OpenGL ES 3.0 in the Android Emulator[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/rendering/using-opengl-es-30.html#enabling-opengl-es-3-0-in-the-android-emulator "Link to this heading")
When you deploy to the Android Emulator an application that uses OpenGL ES API level higher than 2.0, enable OpenGL ES 3.0 in the Android Emulator.
To enable OpenGL ES 3.0 in the Android Emulator:
  1. In Android Studio, in the Device Manager, for the running virtual device, select Extended Controls.
![../../_images/android-studio-device-manager-extended-controls.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/android-studio-device-manager-extended-controls.png)
  2. In the Extended Controls window, select Settings > Advanced. Set the OpenGL ES API level option to Renderer maximum (up to OpenGL ES 3.1).
![../../_images/extended-controls-settings-opengles-api-level.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/extended-controls-settings-opengles-api-level.png)
  3. To apply the changes, restart the Android Emulator.


## See also[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/rendering/using-opengl-es-30.html#sa "Link to this heading")
[Textures](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/textures/textures.html)
[Using render target textures](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/textures/using-render-target-textures.html)
[Shaders](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/shaders/shaders.html)
[Editing shaders](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/shaders/editing-shaders.html)
[Application configuration reference](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/application-configurations/reference-for-application-configuration.html)

# Using the Stack Layout nodes[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/layouts/using-stack-layouts.html#using-the-stack-layout-nodes "Link to this heading")
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/copy-to-clipboard.svg) Copy page ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/arrow-down.svg)

Download and run the Claude mcpb.
Use the Stack Layout nodes to arrange nodes next to each other on the selected axis.
You can set the direction and the starting point for arranging Stack Layout 3D child nodes on x, y, and z axes, and Stack Layout 2D child nodes on x and y axes.
![../../_images/stack-layout.gif](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/stack-layout.gif)
## Creating a Stack Layout node[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/layouts/using-stack-layouts.html#creating-a-stack-layout-node "Link to this heading")
To create a Stack Layout node:
  1. In the Node Tree press `Alt` and right-click the node where you want to create a Stack Layout node and select either Stack Layout 3D, or Stack Layout 2D.
You can create a 3D node only in a 3D node, such as the Scene node, and a 2D node only in a 2D node.
![../../_images/node-tree-create-stack-layout-2d.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/node-tree-create-stack-layout-2d.png)
Tip
In the Preview select the Stack Layout 2D tool ![stack-layout-tool](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/stack-layout-2d-tool.png) to create a Stack Layout 2D node by clicking and dragging in the Preview. The ![stack-tool-arrow](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/stack-tool-arrow.png) above the Stack Layout 2D shows the direction of the layout.
     * When you create a layout whose width is greater than its height, the direction of the layout is on the x axis.
![../../_images/stack-layout-x-axis.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/stack-layout-x-axis.png) ![../../_images/stack-layout-x-direction.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/stack-layout-x-direction.png)
     * When you create a layout whose height is greater than its width, the direction of the layout is on the y axis.
![../../_images/stack-layout-y-axis.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/stack-layout-y-axis.png) ![../../_images/stack-layout-y-direction.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/stack-layout-y-direction.png)
  2. In the Node Tree, add child nodes to the layout that you created in the previous step.
For example, if you created a Stack Layout 3D node, add several Sphere nodes, if you created a Stack Layout 2D node, add several Image nodes.
As you add child nodes, the Stack Layout node positions them along the axis defined by its Direction property.
![../../_images/node-tree-stack-layout-images.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/node-tree-stack-layout-images.png) ![../../_images/preview-stack-layout-images.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/preview-stack-layout-images.png)
  3. (Optional) In the Properties set the Direction property to the axis long which you want the Stack Layout node to arrange its child nodes.
![../../_images/stack-layout-change-direction.gif](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/stack-layout-change-direction.gif)
  4. (Optional) To clear the area around child nodes in a layout, in the Node Tree select child nodes in the layout, in the Properties click ![image0](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/open-add-properties-window.png), and add and set the margin properties:
     * Depth Margin to clear the area in the back and the front of a child node.
     * Horizontal Margin to clear the area on the left and the right sides of a child node.
     * Vertical Margin to clear the area on the bottom and the top of a child node.
![../../_images/stack-layout-add-margin.gif](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/stack-layout-add-margin.gif)


## Reversing the order of Stack Layout node child nodes[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/layouts/using-stack-layouts.html#reversing-the-order-of-stack-layout-node-child-nodes "Link to this heading")
To reverse the order of child nodes in a Stack Layout node, in the Node Tree select the Stack Layout node for which you want to reverse the order of child nodes and in the Properties enable the Reversed property.
![../../_images/stack-layout-reversing-order.gif](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/stack-layout-reversing-order.gif)
## Setting the appearance of a Stack Layout 2D node[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/layouts/using-stack-layouts.html#setting-the-appearance-of-a-stack-layout-2d-node "Link to this heading")
To set the appearance of 2D nodes:
  * You can fill 2D nodes with a solid color, a texture, or a material. See [Adjusting the appearance of 2D nodes](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/2d-content/adjusting-the-appearance.html).
![../../_images/color-brush.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/color-brush.png) ![../../_images/texture-brush.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/texture-brush.png) ![../../_images/material-brush.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/material-brush.png)
  * You can apply a post-processing effect to a 2D node. See [Effects for 2D nodes](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/effects/2d-effects.html).
![../../_images/blur-effect-2d.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/blur-effect-2d.png) ![../../_images/mask-effect-2d.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/mask-effect-2d.png) ![../../_images/outline-effect-2d.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/outline-effect-2d.png) ![../../_images/shadow-effect-2d.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/shadow-effect-2d.png)
  * You can rotate a 2D node around all three axes to create a 3D perspective effect. See [Creating a 3D perspective effect for 2D nodes](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/2d-content/setting-the-perspective.html).
![../../_images/perspective-transformation-visualization.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/perspective-transformation-visualization.png)
  * You can apply custom rendering to 2D nodes to create post-processing effects. See [Applying custom rendering to 2D nodes](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/2d-content/applying-custom-rendering.html).
![../../_images/texture-grayscale.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/texture-grayscale.png)
  * You can render a 2D node as pixel-perfect. See [Rendering pixel-perfect 2D nodes](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/2d-content/adjusting-the-appearance.html#rendering-pixel-perfect-2d-nodes).
![../../_images/snap-to-pixel-icon.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/snap-to-pixel-icon.png)


## Using the Stack Layout 3D node in the API[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/layouts/using-stack-layouts.html#using-the-stack-layout-3d-node-in-the-api "Link to this heading")
To create a Stack Layout 3D node:

```
// Create a Stack Layout 3D node named Stack.
StackLayout3DSharedPtr stack = StackLayout3D::create(domain, "Stack");

```
Copy to clipboard
To control the direction of a Stack Layout 3D node:

```
// Set the Stack Layout 3D node to arrange its items along the x axis.
stack->setDirection(StackLayout3D::DirectionX);

```
Copy to clipboard
To add items to a Stack Layout 3D node:

```
// Stack Layout 3D node arranges its items in the order that you add items.
// Create a Model node and ...
Model3DSharedPtr item1 = Model3D::createBox(domain, "item1", Vector3(1.3f, 1.3f, 1.3f), ThemeRed);
// ... add it to the Stack Layout 3D node.
stack->addChild(item1);
Model3DSharedPtr item2 = Model3D::createSphere(domain, "item2", 0.8f, 30, 30, ThemeGreen);
stack->addChild(item2);
Model3DSharedPtr item3 = Model3D::createBox(domain, "item3", Vector3(1.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f), ThemeBlue);
stack->addChild(item3);

```
Copy to clipboard
To reverse the order in which a Stack Layout 3D node arranges its items:

```
// Set the Stack Layout 3D node to arrange its items in the reverse order.
stack->setReversed(true);

```
Copy to clipboard
For details, see the `StackLayout3D[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a18842.html)` class.
## Using the Stack Layout 2D node in the API[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/layouts/using-stack-layouts.html#using-the-stack-layout-2d-node-in-the-api "Link to this heading")
To create a Stack Layout 2D node:

```
// Create a Stack Layout 2D node named Stack.
StackLayout2DSharedPtr stack = StackLayout2D::create(domain, "Stack");

```
Copy to clipboard
To control the direction of a Stack Layout 2D node:

```
// Set the Stack Layout 2D node to arrange its items along the x axis.
stack->setDirection(StackLayout2D::DirectionX);

```
Copy to clipboard
To add items to a Stack Layout 2D node:

```
// Stack Layout 2D arranges its items in the order that you add items.
// Create a 2D node ...
EmptyNode2DSharedPtr item1 = EmptyNode2D::create(domain, "item1", 100.0f, 100.0f, ThemeRed);
// ... and add it to the Stack Layout 2D node.
stack->addChild(item1);
EmptyNode2DSharedPtr item2 = EmptyNode2D::create(domain, "item2", 100.0f, 100.0f, ThemeGreen);
stack->addChild(item2);
EmptyNode2DSharedPtr item3 = EmptyNode2D::create(domain, "item3", 100.0f, 100.0f, ThemeBlue);
stack->addChild(item3);

```
Copy to clipboard
To reverse the order in which a Stack Layout 2D node arranges its items:

```
// Set the Stack Layout 2D node to arrange its items in the reverse order.
stack->setReversed(true);

```
Copy to clipboard
For details, see the `StackLayout2D[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a18838.html)` class.
##  Stack Layout property types and messages[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/layouts/using-stack-layouts.html#stack-layout-property-types-and-messages "Link to this heading")
For lists of the available property types and messages for the Stack Layout nodes, see [Stack Layout 2D](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/node-and-resource-reference/stack-layout-2d-reference.html) and [Stack Layout 3D](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/node-and-resource-reference/stack-layout-3d-reference.html).

# State manager[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/state-managers.html#state-manager "Link to this heading")
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/copy-to-clipboard.svg) Copy page ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/arrow-down.svg)

![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/claude.svg) Ask Claude
Ask Claude about this topic.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/chatgpt.svg) Ask ChatGPT
Ask ChatGPT about this topic.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/vscode.svg) Connect to VS Code
Install Kanzi Documentation MCP server to VS Code.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/claude.svg) Connect to Claude
Download and run the Claude mcpb.
Use a State Manager to create different states in your Kanzi application.
For example, you can define the appearance and behavior of a button during different states, such as how the button reacts when a user selects, presses, holds, or releases that button. Kanzi uses its animation system to animate the transitions between states. See [Animation system](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/kanzi-fundamentals/animation-system.html).
Each state manager consists:
  * **State groups.** State groups contain states, define controller properties, and transitions between states in a state group. A typical transition defines a period and interpolation paths between property values of two states. You can define transitions using a general guideline for all properties, using interpolations for each property as specified, or using animation items.
  * **States.** Each state contains a collection of properties that define the appearance and behavior of the node to which you assign the state manager. In each state group only one state can be active at a time. A state can also define interactions either by enabling or disabling controls input using the enabled property, setting the state as a condition for the trigger in trigger settings, or by explicitly defining triggers and actions for each state.
  * **State objects.** State objects define the properties of nodes for a specific state. For example, you can assign a state manager to a Button 2D node which contains a Model node that defines the look of the button. State object sets the properties of the mesh set in the Model node using the Target Object Path property. For example, ./Mesh.


For example, a state manager for a button can contain three state groups: button pressed, button released, and hover over button. Each state group contains enabled and disabled states that through state objects define the appearance and behavior of the button when it is in one of the states, and the transition between the states.
You can define the changes between states in these ways:
  * Set a controller property for a state group and a value for that property for each state. These can be implicit properties, such as the Is Down property of the Button nodes. The state changes when the property changes, whether as part of the inherent logic of the node or a specified Set Property action or animation. See [Using a controller property to set states](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-state-managers.html#using-a-controller-property-to-set-states).
  * Using the State Manager actions Go to State, Next State, and Previous State. If you use the State Manager actions and a controller property, note that when the controller property changes, it overrides the previously set state. See [Using state manager actions to set states](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-state-managers.html#using-state-manager-actions-to-set-states).


Learn how to use state managers by completing one of these tutorials:
  * Create a toggle button. See [Tutorial: Creating a toggle button](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/tutorials/toggle-button/toggle-button.html).
  * Create a button and control its state with the Is Down property. See [Tutorial: Creating a button](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/tutorials/button/button.html).
  * Create a turn indicator and control it with a custom property. See [Tutorial: Create cluster indicators](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/tutorials/indicator/indicator.html).


## Easing functions[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/state-managers.html#easing-functions "Link to this heading")
Use an easing function to make UI elements more lifelike. Because objects in real life never start or stop immediately, an appropriate easing function can help you create a more pleasant user experience.
See [Using state transitions](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html).

# Using state transitions[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html#using-state-transitions "Link to this heading")
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/copy-to-clipboard.svg) Copy page ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/arrow-down.svg)

![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/claude.svg) Connect to Claude
Download and run the Claude mcpb.
Use state transitions to define how the state manager reacts when the application state changes, such as when the user clicks a button. For example, you can:
  * Define the duration and start time of a transition
  * Define whether the user can interrupt the transition
  * Use a custom animation. See [Using custom easing functions in state transitions](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html#using-custom-easing-functions-in-state-transitions).


## Setting transitions between any to any state[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html#setting-transitions-between-any-to-any-state "Link to this heading")
When you create states the state manager uses the default transition to transition between states.
To set transitions between any to any state:
  1. Create a node and set the node to use a state manager. See [Using state managers](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-state-managers.html) or [Tutorial: Creating a toggle button](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/tutorials/toggle-button/toggle-button.html).
For example, create a toggle button and a state manager that has one state group with the states On and Off.
  2. In the State Tools click Transition Editor to open the State Transition Editor.
To create a new transition, click + Create Transition under the existing transitions.
![../../_images/open-state-transition-editor1.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/open-state-transition-editor1.png)
  3. When you first open the State Transition Editor it shows the transition that is used between all states in that state group. Move your mouse pointer over ![image0](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/state-transition-editor-c.png) to see the details of the transition.
![../../_images/set-transition-between-any-to-any-state.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/set-transition-between-any-to-any-state.png)
  4. In the popup window set:
     * Duration to the length of the transition in milliseconds.
Either click and drag in the Duration area or enter the new value to set the duration of the transition.
     * Allow interrupt or Always full time set how Kanzi handles interruption of the transition:
       * Always full time uses the entire time set in the Duration to transition to the state after the interruption occurs.
       * Allow interrupt uses only the remaining time set in the Duration to transition to the state after the interruption occurs.
     * Configure Animations enables you to further define the details of the transition. In the State Transition Settings window set:
       * Start Time to the time in milliseconds that elapses before the transition starts.
       * Direction to whether the transition applies to the transition from the Start State to the End State, or to the transitions from both states:
         * Unidirectional applies the transition only to the transition from the Start State to the End State.
         * Bidirectional applies the transition to the transition from the Start State to the End State, and from the End State to the Start State.
       * Easing Function sets the easing function that defines the curve of the transition.
Use an easing function to make UI elements more lifelike. Because objects in real life never start or stop immediately, an appropriate easing function can help you create a more pleasant user experience.
Select the most suitable easing function.
Hover over the image of an easing function to see the type of animation that it creates.

| [ ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/sine-in.png) ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/sine-in.gif) ](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html)  | [ ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/sine-out.png) ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/sine-out.gif) ](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html)  | [ ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/sine-in-out.png) ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/sine-in-out.gif) ](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html)  |  
| **Smoother step**  |   |   |  
| Ease in, Ease out  | Ease in out  |   |  
| [ ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/smoother-step-in.png) ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/smoother-step-in.gif) ](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html)  | [ ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/smoother-step-in-out.png) ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/smoother-step-in-out.gif) ](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html)  |   |  
| **Smooth step**  |   |   |

| [ ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/smooth-step-in.png) ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/smooth-step-in.gif) ](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html)  | [ ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/smooth-step-in-out.png) ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/smooth-step-in-out.gif) ](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html)  |   |  
| **Step**  |   |   |  
| Ease in, Ease out  | Ease in out  |   |  
| [ ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/step-in.png) ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/step-in.gif) ](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html)  | [ ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/step-out.png) ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/step-out.gif) ](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html)  | [ ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/step-in-out.png) ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/multimedia/working-with/animations/step-in-out.gif) ](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html)  |  
       * Easing Mode defines how the easing function is applied to the transition:
         * Ease in applies to the transition the easing function as it is.
         * Ease out applies to the transition the negative value of the easing function.
         * Ease in-out applies to the first half of the transition the easing function as it is, and to the second half of the transition the negative value of the easing function.
       * Transition Animations enables you to use a custom animation for the transition. See [Using custom easing functions in state transitions](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html#using-custom-easing-functions-in-state-transitions).
![../../_images/state-transition-editor-window.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/state-transition-editor-window.png)


## Setting transitions between specific states[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html#setting-transitions-between-specific-states "Link to this heading")
You can set custom transitions between specific states. You can add states to the State Transition Editor canvas and configure transition settings between them.
To set transitions between specific states:
  1. In the State Transition Editor right-click, select Add State To Canvas, and select the state for which you want to set the transitions.
To show all states, right-click and select Add All States To Canvas.
![../../_images/add-state-to-canvas.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/add-state-to-canvas.png)
  2. Click the state to select it and click the Default transitions to set a Custom transition.
![../../_images/state-transition-editor-default-transitions.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/state-transition-editor-default-transitions.png)
  3. Move your mouse pointer over the ![image1](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/state-transition-editor-c.png) transitions to see the details of the transitions.
In the State Tools you see the transitions that you define in the State Transition Editor. To edit the settings for a transition, click that transition.
![../../_images/select-a-transition-in-state-tools.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/select-a-transition-in-state-tools.png) ![../../_images/click-transition-to-open-editor.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/click-transition-to-open-editor.png)


## Using custom easing functions in state transitions[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html#using-custom-easing-functions-in-state-transitions "Link to this heading")
You can use animations to define custom easing functions for transitions between states. For example, define a custom easing function to make a phone call alert blink when you enter that state.
To use custom easing functions in state transitions:
  1. Create or select a node that uses a state manager. See [Using state managers](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-state-managers.html) or [Tutorial: Creating a toggle button](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/tutorials/toggle-button/toggle-button.html).
For example:
    1. Create an Image node that shows the image that alerts the user about an incoming phone call.
![../../_images/incoming-call1.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/incoming-call1.png) ![../../_images/image-in-project.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/image-in-project.png) ![../../_images/image-incoming-call.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/image-incoming-call.png)
    2. Create for the Image node a state manager that has one state group with the states Default and Incoming Call, and add and set the value of the Opacity property of the Image node for each state:
       * For the Default state set it to 0 This way you hide the incoming call image in the Default state when the phone is not ringing.
       * For the Incoming Call state set it to 1 This way you show the incoming call image in the Incoming Call state when the phone is ringing.
![../../_images/image-state-manager.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/image-state-manager.png)
  2. Create an Animation or Animation Clip resource. You use this animation to change the value of the property that you use in the states which you created in the previous step. See [Creating keyframe animations](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/animations/animating-property-values.html).
For example, in the Library > Animations > Animation Data create an Animation that animates the Opacity property of a node. You use this animation to make the node blink three times when the node enters the Incoming Call state.
![../../_images/animation-data-animation-library.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/animation-data-animation-library.png) ![../../_images/animation-target-property-opacity.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/animation-target-property-opacity.png) ![../../_images/animation-clip-editor-opacity-animation.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/animation-clip-editor-opacity-animation.png)
  3. In the Node Tree select the node that you created in the first step and in the State Tools click Any -> Any to open the State Transition Settings.
![../../_images/state-tools-click-any-to-any.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/state-tools-click-any-to-any.png)
  4. In the State Transition Settings set:
     * Start State to the state the transition from which you want to animate
For example, set it to Default.
     * End State to the state the transition to which you want to animate
For example, set it to Incoming Call.
![../../_images/set-start-and-end-state.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/set-start-and-end-state.png)
  5. At the bottom of the State Transition Settings click ![image2](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/add-animation-button.png) to add a transition animation and in the Transition Animations set:
     * Property Type to the property that you want to animate
For example, set it to Opacity.
Kanzi Studio shows in the Property Type dropdown menu only the properties with different values in the Start State and End State states.
     * Easing Function to Custom
     * Custom Animation to the animation that you created earlier in this procedure
For example, set it to Animation.
![../../_images/transition-animation-custom.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/transition-animation-custom.png)


## Configuring easing functions[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html#configuring-easing-functions "Link to this heading")
You can configure some of the easing functions in the State Transition Settings to define the values in the function that sets the transition curve.
The easing functions that you can configure in the State Transition Settings are:
  * Back
    * Use the Amplitude property to sets the amplitude or depth of the transition curve.
![../../_images/back-amplitude.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/back-amplitude.png)
  * Elastic
    * Use the Oscillations property to set the amount of oscillations in the transition curve.
    * Use the Springiness property to set the elasticity of the oscillations in the transition curve.
![../../_images/elastic-oscillations.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/elastic-oscillations.png)
  * Exponential
    * Use the Exponent property to set the exponent to the power of which the transition curve multiplies.
![../../_images/exponential-exponent.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/exponential-exponent.png)
  * Power
    * Use the Power property to set the speed by which the transition curve accelerates.
![../../_images/power.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/power.png)


## Crossfading animations between states[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html#crossfading-animations-between-states "Link to this heading")
When the states in a state group contain Animation Player node components with the same name, the State Manager automatically crossfades between the outgoing and incoming animations over the transition duration. The crossfade uses a linear blend regardless of the easing function configured on the transition.
See [Blending animations](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/animations/blending-animations.html).
## See also[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-transitions.html#sa "Link to this heading")
[State manager](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/state-managers.html)
[Using state managers](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/state-managers/using-state-managers.html)
[Blending animations](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/animations/blending-animations.html)
[Tutorial: Creating a toggle button](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/tutorials/toggle-button/toggle-button.html)
[Using the Button nodes](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/buttons/using-buttons.html)

# Using styles[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/styles/using-styles.html#using-styles "Link to this heading")
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/copy-to-clipboard.svg) Copy page ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/arrow-down.svg)
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/copy-to-clipboard.svg) Copy page
Copy this page as Markdown for LLMs.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/markdown.svg) View as Markdown
View this page as Markdown.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/claude.svg) Ask Claude
Ask Claude about this topic.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/chatgpt.svg) Ask ChatGPT
Ask ChatGPT about this topic.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/vscode.svg) Connect to VS Code
Install Kanzi Documentation MCP server to VS Code.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/claude.svg) Connect to Claude
Download and run the Claude mcpb.
Use styles to set the property values of one or more nodes of a certain type.
In a style you set the values of properties the style applies to a node. For example, use a style to define the font type, size, and color of the text for all Text Block 3D nodes in your project.
To override a property defined in a style, add that property to the node to which the style applies.
Using styles you can:
  * Create a target style that applies to a specific branch of nodes in your Kanzi Studio project. See [Applying a style that applies to a node type in the selected scope](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/styles/using-styles.html#applying-a-style-that-applies-to-a-node-type-in-the-selected-scope).
  * Create a named style that applies to selected instances of a certain node type, or overrides the target styles. See [Applying a style to selected instances of a node type](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/styles/using-styles.html#applying-a-style-to-selected-instances-of-a-node-type).


## Applying a style that applies to a node type in the selected scope[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/styles/using-styles.html#applying-a-style-that-applies-to-a-node-type-in-the-selected-scope "Link to this heading")
Target styles define the look and feel for a selected node type in a specific part of the node tree in a Kanzi Studio project.
For example, to use different font sizes for the text at different levels of navigation, create a style for each navigation level, and add each style to the resource dictionary at each level of navigation.
To apply a style to descendants of a node type:
  1. In the Library press `Alt` and right-click Styles and select Typed Style.
![../../_images/create-typed-style.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/create-typed-style.png)
  2. In the Properties set the Target Type property to the node type for which you want to define a style.
For example, set Target Type to Text Block 2D to define a style for Text Block 2D nodes in your project.
![../../_images/set-target-type.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/set-target-type.png)
  3. In the Properties click ![add-properties](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/open-add-properties-window.png), and add and set the properties you want to define with the style.
For example, to define the color of font for a Text Block 2D node, add the Foreground Brush property, and set it to a brush you want to use to render the text in the Text Block 2D node.
![../../_images/foreground-brush.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/foreground-brush.png)
  4. In the Node Tree press `Alt` and right-click the node to whose descendants you want to apply the style and select Resource Dictionary.
![../../_images/select-resource-dictionary.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/select-resource-dictionary.png)
  5. In the Dictionaries in the scope of the node to whose descendants you want to apply the style, click + Add Resource, select Add Existing, and select the style you created.
![../../_images/add-existing-typed-style.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/add-existing-typed-style.png)
  6. If the properties you defined in the style exist in the target nodes, remove them from the target nodes so that the style can take effect.
  7. By default the Text Block 2D nodes use the Text Block 2D Style which sets the Snap to Pixel property.
The Snap to Pixel property rounds the translation and scale of a Text Block 2D or Text Box 2D node to a full pixel, which enables Kanzi to render pixel-perfect text.
To enable the Snap to Pixel property for the Text Block 2D node you created, add the Snap to Pixel property to the Typed Style you created.
![../../_images/typed-style-snap-to-pixel-added.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/typed-style-snap-to-pixel-added.png)


## Applying a style to selected instances of a node type[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/styles/using-styles.html#applying-a-style-to-selected-instances-of-a-node-type "Link to this heading")
Named styles define the look and feel only for the selected instances of a node type, or override the target styles. For example, if you create a target style for the Text Block 3D, you can override that style with a named style.
To apply a style to only selected instances of a node type:
  1. In the Library press `Alt` and right-click Styles and select Named Style.
![../../_images/create-named-style.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/create-named-style.png)
  2. In the Properties set the Target Type property to the node type for which you want to define a style.
For example, set Target Type to Text Block 3D to define a style for Text Block 3D nodes in your project.
![../../_images/set-target-type-for-named-style.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/set-target-type-for-named-style.png)
  3. In the Properties click ![add-properties](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/open-add-properties-window.png), and add and set the properties you want to define with the style.
For example, to define the color of font for a Text Block 3D node, add the Font Color property and set it to red.
![../../_images/font-color.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/font-color.png)
  4. In the Node Tree select the node to the instance of which you want to apply the style, in the Properties click ![add-properties](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/open-add-properties-window.png), add the Style property, and set it to a named style.
![../../_images/add-the-style-property.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/add-the-style-property.png)
  5. If the properties you defined in the style exist in the target nodes, remove them from the target nodes so that the style can take effect.


## Using styles in the API[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/styles/using-styles.html#using-styles-in-the-api "Link to this heading")
For details, see the `Style[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a14622.html)` class.
##  Style property types[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/styles/using-styles.html#style-property-types "Link to this heading")
For a list of the available property types for styles, see [Style](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/node-and-resource-reference/style-reference.html).
## See also[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/styles/using-styles.html#sa "Link to this heading")

# Using tags[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/tags/using-tags.html#using-tags "Link to this heading")
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/copy-to-clipboard.svg) Copy page ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/arrow-down.svg)

![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/claude.svg) Connect to Claude
Download and run the Claude mcpb.
Use tags to group, find, and filter nodes in your project. You can assign multiple tags to a single node.
For example, you can use tags to:
  * Find nodes using the quick search in the Node Tree. See [Finding tagged nodes in the Node Tree](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/tags/using-tags.html#finding).
  * Find nodes using the Find Project Item tool. See [Finding tagged nodes using the Find Project Item tool](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/tags/using-tags.html#finding2).
  * Render only specific nodes in your project. See [Using the Tag Filter](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/filters/using-tag-filters.html).


## Tagging a node[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/tags/using-tags.html#tagging-a-node "Link to this heading")
You can create a tag and tag a node in the Properties of that node.
To tag a node:
  1. In the Node Tree select the node you want to tag.
  2. In the Properties:
     * In the Tags property enter the name of the tag and press `Enter`.
Kanzi Studio creates the tag and tags the node with the tag.
![../../_images/create-tag-tags-property.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/create-tag-tags-property.png)
     * Click the Tags button next to the Tags property and select a tag from the list of existing tags.
Kanzi Studio uses the existing tag to tag the node.
![../../_images/use-exisiting-tag.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/use-exisiting-tag.png)


## Creating a tag without tagging a node[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/tags/using-tags.html#creating-a-tag-without-tagging-a-node "Link to this heading")
You can create a tag without tagging a node at the same time.
To create a tag without tagging a node:
  1. In the Library press `Alt` and right-click Tags and select Tag.
![../../_images/create-tag.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/create-tag.png)
  2. Name the tag and click OK.
Kanzi Studio creates the tag and lists it in the Library > Tags.
![../../_images/tags-in-library-tags.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/tags-in-library-tags.png)


## Finding tagged nodes in the Node Tree[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/tags/using-tags.html#finding-tagged-nodes-in-the-node-tree "Link to this heading")
To find tagged nodes in the Node Tree:
  1. Create a tag and assign it to nodes. See [Tagging a node](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/tags/using-tags.html#tagging-a-node).
  2. In the Node Tree, in the search box, enter the tag name that you are looking for.
The Node Tree shows only the nodes that contain the tag you entered in the search box.


## Finding tagged nodes using the Find Project Item tool[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/tags/using-tags.html#finding-tagged-nodes-using-the-find-project-item-tool "Link to this heading")
To find tagged nodes using the Find Project Item tool:
  1. Create a tag and assign it to nodes. See [Tagging a node](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/tags/using-tags.html#tagging-a-node).
  2. Select Edit > Find.
The Find Project Item window opens.
![../../_images/edit-find.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/edit-find.png)
  3. In the Advanced Search tab in the Criteria section click ![image0](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/add-property.png) to add a new criterion and in the criterion:
    1. Select Has Property Value.
    2. Select the Tags property.
    3. Click the Tags button and select the tag you are looking for.
![../../_images/find-tag-criterion.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/find-tag-criterion.png)
  4. Click Search.
The Find Project Item shows all nodes with the tag you selected.
![../../_images/search-tag.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/search-tag.png)


## Using tags in the API[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/tags/using-tags.html#using-tags-in-the-api "Link to this heading")
For details, see the `Node[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a13774.html)` tag interface. The relevant functions are `Node::acquireTag[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a13774.html#acbda97d5353f6eb11c0e5b772860c9cc)`, `Node::hasTag[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a13774.html#abad675424d292038276131ceba09060c)`, `Node::setTag[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a13774.html#aaf59eb73970df1d7f597391b86057f9f)` and `Node::removeTag[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a13774.html#a3b5071a0afeaba1c92f3fe20667fe132)`.

# Text[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/text/text.html#text "Link to this heading") ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/copy-to-clipboard.svg) Copy page ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/arrow-down.svg) ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/copy-to-clipboard.svg) Copy page Copy this page as Markdown for LLMs. ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/markdown.svg) View as Markdown View this page as Markdown. ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/claude.svg) Ask Claude Ask Claude about this topic. ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/chatgpt.svg) Ask ChatGPT Ask ChatGPT about this topic. ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/vscode.svg) Connect to VS Code Install Kanzi Documentation MCP server to VS Code. ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/claude.svg) Connect to Claude Download and run the Claude mcpb. Kanzi has these text nodes: * Use the Text Block nodes to show a small amount of text in your application. See [Using the Text Block nodes](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/text/using-text-blocks.html). ![../../_images/text-blcok-2d-icon.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/text-blcok-2d-icon.png) * Use the Text Box nodes to add single-line text input to your application. See [Using the Text Box nodes](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/text/using-text-boxes.html). ![../../_images/text-box-2d-icon.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/text-box-2d-icon.png) ## Font type[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/text/text.html#font-type "Link to this heading") The default font family in Kanzi is [Fira Sans Regular](https://mozilla.github.io/Fira/). The font file is stored in `/Studio/Asset Library/Fonts`. When you want to use your own font, import it to your Kanzi Studio project. See [Importing fonts](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/importing/importing-fonts.html). You can use these font types in your Kanzi applications: * TrueType and OpenType fonts (ttf and otf files) * iType linked fonts (ltt files). See [iType linked fonts](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/importing/importing-fonts.html#itype-linked-fonts). * Bitmap fonts (fnt files). See [Using bitmap fonts](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/importing/importing-fonts.html#using-bitmap-fonts). Make sure that the font you use includes all the glyphs for the text that you want to include in your Kanzi application. ## Font size[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/text/text.html#font-size "Link to this heading") Kanzi sets the size of fonts in pixels. When you set the Font Size property, Kanzi passes that value to the Freetype library, which Kanzi uses to render fonts, using the [FT_Set_Char_Size](https://www.freetype.org/freetype2/docs/reference/ft2-base_interface.html#FT_Set_Char_Size) function with the default dpi value of 72. For example, both of these display the letter H of the same size: * Text Block or Text Box nodes with these properties set: * Text to H * Font Family to Arial * Font Size to 36 * HTML markup ```

H

``` Copy to clipboard If you want to control the dpi scaling or set the font size in units other than pixels, you must implement that functionality in your Kanzi application. For example, if you want to automatically select the content that the images and layouts in your project use based on the dpi setting, implement that functionality in your Kanzi application. ## Setting the font engine for the Preview[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/text/text.html#setting-the-font-engine-for-the-preview "Link to this heading") You can set which font engine you want the Kanzi Studio Preview to use to render the text in your application. To set the font engine for the Preview: 1. In the main menu select Project > Properties. ![../../_images/project-properties.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/project-properties.png) 2. In the Properties set the Font Engine property: * FreeType uses the FreeType rasterizer, HarfBuzz shaper, and ICU bidirectional library, and libunibreak for line breaking. This is the default font engine. * iType uses the Monotype iType rasterizer and WorldType® Shaper™ for shaping. See [Installing the iType font engine](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/preview/controlling-your-application-in-the-preview.html#installing-the-itype-font-engine). * None to not load a font engine. When you do not load a font engine, the Preview does not render the text in your application. ![../../_images/font-engine.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/font-engine.png) To learn how to set which font engine to load at application startup, see [FontEngine](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/application-configurations/reference-for-application-configuration.html#fontengine). ## Setting font hinting[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/text/text.html#setting-font-hinting "Link to this heading") Font hinting provides instructions for rasterization: mapping the outlines of fonts to screen pixels. Font hinting aims to both maintain the design aesthetic of a font and optimize the readability of the font at different sizes. Text nodes in Kanzi by default use the font hinting data included in a font. For example, font hinting can affect the height and width of characters, the width of lines, edge contrast, and the space between characters. To set font hinting for a Text Block or Text Box node, in the Node Tree select that node, in the Properties add the Font Hinting Preference property, and set it to: * No hinting to render text without font hinting. * Native hinting to render text using the hinting data included in the font. If the font does not contain hinting data, Kanzi uses the hinter of the font engine rasterizer. This is the default value. * Auto hinting to render text using the hinter of the font engine rasterizer. See [Setting the font engine for the Preview](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/text/text.html#setting-font-engine-for-preview). ![../../_images/font-hinting-preference.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/font-hinting-preference.png) ## Font fallback[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/text/text.html#font-fallback "Link to this heading") In Kanzi, you can define a Fallback Font Chain for a Font Family. If a character is not available in the current font, Kanzi searches the fallback font chain in order, selecting the first font family that contains the missing character. If the character is not found in any fallback font family, the glyph with **glyph ID 0** in the current font is used as the missing glyph character. Use fallback fonts to: * Display multiple languages in a single text node. * Show special characters like emojis and symbols alongside regular text. When rendering with a fallback font, Kanzi attempts to select a font file from the fallback family that closely matches the style and weight of the current font. To optimize performance and memory usage, fallback fonts are only loaded when a character is not found in the current font or any of the earlier fallback fonts in the chain. To configure the Fallback Font Chain, you can choose from existing font families using the dropdown menu, or add a font family using a kzb URL. ![../../_images/font-fallbacks.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/font-fallbacks.png) ## Color fonts[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/text/text.html#color-fonts "Link to this heading") To render emoji and other colored glyphs, import a font file that contains color glyphs. The color font file can be either the primary font of a Font Family or a fallback font. These color font formats are supported for each Kanzi font engine: | Font file type | FreeType | iType | | --- | --- | --- | | glyf table (normal non-colored scalable text and icons) | ✅ | ✅ | | CBDT table (non-scalable PNG images) | ✅ | ✅ | | SBIX table (non-scalable PNG images) | ✅ | ❌ | | COLRv0 table (scalable shapes with solid colors) | ✅ | ✅ | | SVG table (SVG images with color gradients) | ❌ | ❌ | | COLRv1 table (scalable shapes with color gradients) | ❌ | ❌ | When you use a font file that contains glyphs in a non-supported font format: * If the font file contains glyphs in multiple formats, Kanzi uses non-colored version of the glyphs * Kanzi does not render the glyphs Note Kanzi renders colored glyphs using a different brush and material than normal text. This material uses only the alpha channel of the Foreground Brush property color (Font Color property for 3D text). This means that you can change the color of text without affecting the emoji colors. ![../../_images/color-fonts.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/color-fonts.png) ## Customizing word wrapping in Thai text with iType font engine[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/text/text.html#customizing-word-wrapping-in-thai-text-with-itype-font-engine "Link to this heading") You can customize how Kanzi iType font engine wraps words in Thai text by setting a Thai dictionary that you want to use instead of the one that is built into the iType font engine. WorldType® SDK comes with: * Thai dictionary * Python utility that creates a Thai dictionary that your application can use You can find these resources in the WorldType® SDK in the `wtle/product/tools/language_dictionaries/thai` directory. To wrap words automatically in Thai text: 1. Create a Thai dictionary for the iType font engine by passing to `GenerateThaiDictionary.py`: * Thai dictionary in plain-text format * File where you want to store the generated dictionary ``` py -2 GenerateThaiDictionary.py thai-dictionary.txt thai-dictionary.wtd ``` Copy to clipboard `GenerateThaiDictionary.py` creates a wtd file that you set in the application configuration of your Kanzi application: ``` Reading lines from file "thai-dictionary.txt"... done. Extracting, filtering, and normalizing words... done. Adding words to trie... done. number of words: 8 number of characters: 31 longest word length: 7 number of trie nodes: 32 number of trie edges: 31 Compressing trie into a DAWG (Directed Acyclic Word Graph)... done. number of edges in root node: 9 number of DAWG nodes: 24 number of DAWG edges: 30 edges / characters = 96.8 % dawgEdges / trieEdges = 96.0 % dawgNodes / trieNodes = 75.0 % DAWG array elements: 31 Writing DAWG to file "thai-dictionary.wtd"... done. file size: 0 k ``` Copy to clipboard 2. To set your application to use the Thai dictionary that you created, in a text editor set the iType font engine dictionary in the `/Application/bin/application.cfg` file: ``` # Set additional backend dictionaries. ITypeDictionaryUrls = file:///usr/share/itype/thai-dictionary.wtd ``` Copy to clipboard See [Font engine dictionaries](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/application-configurations/reference-for-application-configuration.html#font-engine-dictionaries). 3. (Optional) To set the Kanzi Studio Preview to correctly render Thai text when you use the iType font engine, in Kanzi Studio open your project and in the main menu select Project > Properties. In the Properties set the Preview Working Directory property to the directory that contains the `application.cfg` file that you created in the previous step. ![../../_images/project-properties.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/project-properties.png) ![../../_images/properties-preview-working-directory.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/properties-preview-working-directory.png) ## See also[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/text/text.html#sa "Link to this heading") [Using the Text Block nodes](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/text/using-text-blocks.html) [Using the Text Box nodes](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/text/using-text-boxes.html) [Importing fonts](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/importing/importing-fonts.html) [Glyph cache texture size](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/application-configurations/reference-for-application-configuration.html#glyph-cache-texture-size)

# Textures[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/textures/textures.html#textures "Link to this heading")
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/copy-to-clipboard.svg) Copy page ![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/arrow-down.svg)
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/copy-to-clipboard.svg) Copy page
Copy this page as Markdown for LLMs.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/markdown.svg) View as Markdown
View this page as Markdown.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/claude.svg) Ask Claude
Ask Claude about this topic.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/chatgpt.svg) Ask ChatGPT
Ask ChatGPT about this topic.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/vscode.svg) Connect to VS Code
Install Kanzi Documentation MCP server to VS Code.
![](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_static/claude.svg) Connect to Claude
Download and run the Claude mcpb.
Use textures to show content in Image nodes, to set the look of textured materials, and to show content in Texture Brush brushes. You can create textures from common image file formats.
See [Images](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/images/images.html).
In a Kanzi Studio project, image files are located in Library > Resource Files > Images. These image files correspond to files on your hard drive. When you modify a file on the hard drive, Kanzi automatically applies the modifications to the textures generated from that file. If you remove the file from the hard drive, you cannot use the file in your Kanzi project.
![../../_images/resource-files-images-defaulttextureimage.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/resource-files-images-defaulttextureimage.png)
Loading time of images depends on their size and compression:
  * **Image size** defines the time required to load the data into RAM.
  * **Image compression** can reduce the size, but keep in mind that before your application can use the image, it must decompress it, which is often slower than loading the raw data. You can often achieve the fastest start-up times when using Raw image format, where data is loaded into RAM and sent to the GPU memory. See [Image Compression](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/images/images.html#image-compression).
  * **Texture compression** you can use on devices with GPUs that support the selected compression algorithm. When using compression, the data size is smaller both when loading from kzb file to RAM and when loading from RAM to the GPU memory. Also less GPU memory is reserved. Depending on the target hardware, by using texture compression you can reduce loading times. Before using texture compression, make sure that your target platform supports the texture compression format you selected.
Kanzi supports ASTC, ETC, and BCn compression formats.
If your target hardware does not support the selected texture compression algorithm, when you run your Kanzi application on your target device, Kanzi prints a warning message to the log. Kanzi paints black the surfaces where you use compressed texture formats that your target hardware does not support.
See [Compressing textures](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/best-practices/images-and-textures/compressing-textures.html).


## Texture types[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/textures/textures.html#texture-types "Link to this heading")
These textures are available in Kanzi:  
|  Single textures use a single image for the texture. See [Using single textures](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/textures/using-single-textures.html).  |  ![../../_images/single-texture.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/single-texture.png)  |  
| --- | --- |  
|  Cubemap textures combine six square-shaped images into one texture to represent reflections of the environment. Each image represents the scenery in one of the six directions along the x, y, and z axes from the viewpoint of the cubemapped object. See [Using cubemap textures](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/textures/using-cubemap-textures.html).  |  ![../../_images/cubemap-texture.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/cubemap-texture.png)  |  
|  Volume textures use a single 2D image, made up of many cross-section slices of a 3D shape, to define a 3D volume texture. This technique is often used for effects like smoke, fire, or clouds, where 3D data would be too resource intensive or difficult to generate procedurally. See [Using volume textures](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/textures/using-volume-textures.html).  |  ![../../_images/volume-texture.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/volume-texture.png)  |  
|  Use a Render Target Texture to render content to a texture or to apply anti-aliasing to only a part of your application. You can use render target textures like any other texture. For example, you can use it in a Texture Brush or as an image in an Image node. See [Using render target textures](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/textures/using-render-target-textures.html) and [Using OpenGL ES 3.0+ in Kanzi](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/rendering/using-opengl-es-30.html).  |  ![../../_images/render-target-texture.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/render-target-texture.png)  |  
|  Use a Cubemap Render Target Texture to render a Cubemap render pass to a cubemap texture. See [Creating cubemap reflections](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/rendering/cubemap-render-pass.html).  |  ![../../_images/cubemap-render-target-texture.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/cubemap-render-target-texture.png)  |  
You can use .exr, .dds, and .hdr images with half float and floating point data to bring HDR images to your Kanzi project. See [Setting the color format of textures](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/rendering/using-opengl-es-30.html#setting-the-color-format-of-textures).
## Setting the image target format[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/textures/textures.html#setting-the-image-target-format "Link to this heading")
When you export your project to a kzb file, Kanzi Studio reads the images in the project using the format of the original image and writes the images to a kzb file in the format you set with the Target Format property for each image.
If the file format of the original image is the same as the format you select in the Target Format property, Kanzi Studio does not modify the image when it writes the image to a kzb file under these conditions:
  * Premultiply Alpha is disabled, or the alpha channel does not need to be premultiplied
To change this setting, in the Project > Properties use the Premultiply Alpha property. You can override this value in the properties of the image file where you want to use a different setting.
![../../_images/premultiply-alpha-project.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/premultiply-alpha-project.png) ![../../_images/premultiply-alpha-image.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/premultiply-alpha-image.png)
  * Generate Mipmaps is disabled
You can set the value of the Generate Mipmaps property in each image file.
![../../_images/generate-mipmaps-disabled.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/generate-mipmaps-disabled.png)
  * Round up Image Dimensions to Nearest Power of Two property is disabled
You can set the value of the Round up Image Dimensions to Nearest Power of Two property in the Project > Properties.
When you enable the Round up Image Dimensions to Nearest Power of Two property, Kanzi Studio rounds up the width and height of the images in your project to the nearest power of two during kzb file export. For example, Kanzi Studio exports an image of the size 40 by 30 pixels to the kzb file in the size 64 by 32 pixels.
![../../_images/round-images-to-nearest-power-of-2-disabled.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/round-images-to-nearest-power-of-2-disabled.png)


If your image is in JPEG or PNG format and you do not want Kanzi Studio to modify the image that it exports to a kzb file, in the image Properties enable the Use Original Image property.
![../../_images/use-original-image-enabled.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/use-original-image-enabled.png)
To set the image target format:
  1. In the Library > Resource Files > Images select the image for which you want to set the target format.
![../../_images/resource-files-images-defaulttextureimage.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/resource-files-images-defaulttextureimage.png)
  2. In the Properties set the Target Format property to the image format you want to use in your Kanzi application.
The format you select is important because this influences the size of the kzb file and the loading time when your Kanzi application loads the image. Make sure that your target device supports the target format you select for the image. See [Images and textures best practices](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/best-practices/images-and-textures/images-and-textures-best-practices.html) and [Compressing textures](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/best-practices/images-and-textures/compressing-textures.html).
![../../_images/target-format-astc-compression.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/target-format-astc-compression.png)
  3. If the image format you selected in the previous step supports compression, configure the compression scheme you want to use. See [Compressing textures](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/best-practices/images-and-textures/compressing-textures.html).
![../../_images/astc-block-size.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/astc-block-size.png)
  4. For image formats that support sRGB:
     * If the image contains sRGB color information, set the sRGB Content property to enabled. This is the default setting.
If you disable the sRGB Content property for an image that contains sRGB color information, Kanzi can render the textures that use the image brighter than expected.
     * If the image contains non-color information, such as a normal, roughness, or occlusion map, set the sRGB Content property to disabled.
Textures that contain non-color information are stored in linear format. By disabling the sRGB Content property you set Kanzi to pass the image data to a shader directly, without performing a color space conversion.
![../../_images/srgb-content.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/srgb-content.png)
  5. If you want Kanzi to premultiply the alpha channel in the:
     * Linear color space, set the Linear Premultiply property to enabled.
This is the default value and results in the fewest artifacts in sRGB images.
     * Color space of the image, usually sRGB, set the Linear Premultiply property to disabled.
This can give better results for images created for the standard color workflow.
See [Preparing images in third-party tools](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/images/preparing-images-in-3rd-party-tools.html).
![../../_images/linear-premultiply.png](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/_images/linear-premultiply.png)


## Using textures in the API[¶](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/working-with/textures/textures.html#using-textures-in-the-api "Link to this heading")
For details, see the `Texture[](https://docs.kanzi.com/4.1.0/en/reference/kanzi-runtime-api/a12570.html)` class.
